sections.heading: Coming to Christ and nowhere else
sections.text: Lord God, you have called me to trust in Jesus, and I do. Keep pulling my heart away from every false place I run for safety. I do not want another refuge, another cleansing, another foundation, another source of life, or another place to rest. Let Jesus be enough for me—not just in what I say I believe, but in what I actually depend on when I am afraid, guilty, tired, or tempted.
theological_themes: God commands and enables faith in Christ
Christ alone is the sinner’s refuge, cleansing, foundation, fullness, and rest
Exclusive trust in Jesus rather than self-made securities

scripture_references.connection: Peter declares that salvation is found in no one but Jesus. This supports the prayer’s refusal to seek refuge, cleansing, or rescue anywhere else.
Paul teaches that no foundation can be laid other than Jesus Christ. The prayer’s language of building on no other foundation rests on this same Christ-centered confidence.

sections.heading: Receiving both forgiveness and cleansing
sections.text: Father, at the cross Jesus gave himself completely. Do not let me separate what you have joined together. Make me deeply honest about both the guilt of my sin and the way sin stains and twists me. I need Jesus not only to pardon me, but to change me. Give me repentance as well as forgiveness. Teach me to love what is holy, to want a clean heart, to think with the mind of Christ, and to walk in the path he walked.
theological_themes: Christ’s saving work addresses both guilt and corruption
Repentance and forgiveness are gifts found in Christ
Holiness is inseparable from the gospel
The believer is called to Christlike life and obedience

scripture_references.connection: This passage presents Jesus as the exalted Leader and Savior who gives both repentance and forgiveness. That directly grounds the prayer’s request for inward turning as well as pardon.

Paul says Christ gave himself to redeem and purify a people zealous for good works. The prayer’s concern for forgiveness, cleansing, holiness, and practical obedience reflects this full scope of salvation.
Peter describes Christ’s suffering as leaving believers an example to follow. This supports the prayer’s desire to have Christ’s mind and walk in his steps.

sections.heading: Belonging to your wise and gentle care
sections.text: Do not leave me to run my own life as if I belonged to myself. Help me rejoice that I am in your hands. You are wiser than I am, and you do not make mistakes. You are kinder than my fears imagine, and you do not harm your children. You are gentle with weak people, and you do not crush those who come to you in need. Teach me to rest under your care instead of fighting for control.
theological_themes: The believer belongs to God, not to self
God’s providence is wise, kind, and tender
Surrender grows from trust in God’s character

scripture_references.connection: Paul reminds believers that they are not their own because they were bought with a price. This grounds the prayer’s surrender of self-disposal to God’s ownership and care.
Jesus invites the weary to come to him and describes himself as gentle and lowly. This supports the prayer’s confidence that God’s rule is not crushing but tender and restful.

sections.heading: Living so others can see Christ clearly
sections.text: Please keep my attitude, words, and behavior from making Christ look ugly to the people around me. Let my life make him seem as good and beautiful as he truly is. Wherever I have the chance, help me do real good to others. Do not let me walk past opportunities to serve just because they are inconvenient, unnoticed, or costly.
theological_themes: Christian conduct should adorn the gospel rather than discredit it
Believers are called to active goodness and usefulness
Love for neighbor is a visible witness to Christ

scripture_references.connection: Paul urges believers to live in a way that adorns the doctrine of God our Savior. This matches the prayer’s desire not to scandalize others but to make Christ attractive through conduct.
Paul calls Christians to do good as they have opportunity, especially to fellow believers. That supports the prayer’s request not to refuse chances for usefulness and mercy.

sections.heading: Using what I have as a steward, not an owner
sections.text: Teach me to see my money and possessions rightly. They are not for showing off, feeding pride, or making comfort my god. They are gifts to support the life you have given me and responsibilities you have entrusted to me. Help me govern my desires wisely, live honestly, avoid needless debt, and have enough open-handedness to help those in need. Make mercy and forgiveness feel not like burdens, but like part of the joy of belonging to Jesus. Shape me so that the world sees something of his likeness in me.
theological_themes: Possessions are entrusted by God for stewardship, not pride or luxury
Financial integrity and generosity belong to Christian discipleship
Mercy and forgiveness reflect the character of Christ
The goal of Christian life is conformity to Jesus

scripture_references.connection: Paul’s command to owe no one anything except love directly supports the prayer’s concern for financial integrity while keeping love at the center.
Paul connects honest labor with the ability to share with anyone in need. This grounds the prayer’s desire to handle resources responsibly and generously.
Believers are commanded to be kind, tenderhearted, and forgiving because God has forgiven them in Christ. This supports the prayer’s longing to be merciful and forgiving as a reflection of Jesus.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase about Christ’s “water and blood” not being separated at the cross is theologically rich but interpretively dense. It likely points to Christ’s atoning death and the inseparability of pardon and cleansing, rather than to sacramental theology alone.

The prayer assumes a strong doctrine of providence in which God’s care is always wise, kind, and tender. This is biblically grounded, but pastorally it must be rendered without implying that suffering is painless or that harm done by others should be minimized.

The original’s comments on substance, debt, and giving reflect a moral vision of stewardship and financial integrity. They were retained without turning them into a rigid rule against every form of borrowing.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “prince and saviour” as Jesus being the one who rules, rescues, grants repentance, and forgives, drawing especially on Acts 5:31.

I interpreted “guilt and pollution of sin” as the need for both forgiveness before God and inward cleansing from sin’s corrupting power, preserving the original’s refusal to separate justification from sanctification.
I translated “not be at my own disposal” as belonging to God rather than running my own life, to keep the force of surrender without using archaic phrasing.
I treated “recommend and endear Christ” as living in a way that makes Christ’s goodness visible rather than as a call to manage other people’s opinions.
